title: Sampling Strategies & Sample Representativeness
description: Master probability sampling (random, stratified, cluster) vs. non-probability sampling (convenience, snowball), and response rates.

slides.title: Population vs. Sample 🎯
slides.content:
# Who Are You Really Studying?

In psychological research, we rarely have the resources to test everyone:

* **Population**: The entire, complete group of individuals that a researcher wants to draw conclusions about (e.g., all adolescents aged 13–17 worldwide, or all patients diagnosed with schizophrenia in Canada).
* **Sample**: The subset of individuals selected from the population to participate in the study.
* **Representativeness**: A sample is representative if its key demographic and psychological characteristics mirror the broader population.

A study conducted on 10,000 unrepresentative people is scientifically worthless compared to a study conducted on 500 carefully representative individuals!

quizData.question: A clinical team investigates burnout among all 4,000 nurses employed across a state hospital network by surveying 250 randomly selected nurses. In this study, the 4,000 nurses represent:
quizData.explanation: The entire group of interest (all 4,000 employed nurses) is the population; the 250 selected individuals form the sample.

slides.title: Probability vs. Non-Probability Sampling 🎲
slides.content:
## Methods for Selecting Participants

Sampling methods fall into two major categories:

| Sampling Method | Category | How It Works | Strengths & Limitations |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Simple Random Sampling** | Probability | Every single member of the population has an equal, known chance of selection (e.g., lottery draw from a full registry) | Gold standard for representativeness; requires complete population list. |
| **Stratified Random Sampling** | Probability | Population divided into subgroups (strata: e.g., ethnicity, age), and random samples drawn from each stratum proportionally | Guarantees adequate representation of small minority subgroups. |
| **Cluster Sampling** | Probability | Naturally occurring geographic clusters selected at random (e.g., randomly picking 10 schools, then surveying all students within them) | Cost-effective for geographically dispersed populations. |
| **Convenience Sampling** | Non-Probability | Selecting participants who are easiest to recruit (e.g., college students in an Intro Psych pool) | Cheap and fast; vulnerable to sampling bias and limited generalizability. |
| **Snowball Sampling** | Non-Probability | Existing participants recruit future participants from their acquaintances | Ideal for hidden or stigmatized populations (e.g., undocumented migrants, illicit drug users). |

Most university psychology studies rely on convenience samples, creating the famous **WEIRD** problem.

quizData.question: A psychologist studies a hidden underground community of extreme urban explorers by interviewing two explorers and asking them to introduce her to other members of their network. What sampling technique is this?
quizData.explanation: Snowball sampling relies on word-of-mouth referral chains, which is ideal for locating difficult-to-reach or secretive populations.

slides.title: Methodological Warning ⚠️
slides.content:
### The WEIRD Participant Bias

Over 80% of published psychology research historically sampled populations that are **WEIRD**: *Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic* (primarily American undergraduate students!). Be extremely cautious before claiming a cognitive or perceptual finding applies to all human beings across cultures.
